children: has developed the Life Sciences Verification Program, which grants life science professionals access to its Mythos, Opus, and Sonnet models.

Those approved receive a refined set of safeguards that are more permissive for biology-related work. Anthropic has already onboarded dozens of organizations through an early-access program and is now opening that up to the broader life sciences community. Each applicant must pass a verification process that includes a review of their research credentials, security standards, and ethical research oversight. There is a "standard use" grant and a "high-risk use" grant. The high-risk use removes all safeguards for bio-work and must be renewed every six months.

"Biological misuse is one of the most serious risks of frontier AI models," Anthropic said. "It has long been a concern that AI models might one day reach the level of capability where they can help to make existing pathogens more dangerous—or create entirely new ones."

Anthropic recently identified multiple cases of Claude users engaged in efforts to possibly create new biological weapons. For example, a researcher in an unsupported region spent weeks planning avian influenza mammalian-adaptation experiments with Claude. In another, a state-supported researcher built a venom peptide atlas and generative optimization pipeline of molecules directed at paralytic and analgesic targets. A third attempted to alter an organism genetically to create a new or enhanced biological property with the chikungunya virus, a mosquito-spread disease that attacks the joints.

"In order to defend against these threats and in close collaboration with enterprise CISOs, we designed the new LSVP safeguards around the concept of shared responsibility by monitoring usage against the intended use case for the model access," according to Anthropic. "Because we vet the LSVP organizations for their life sciences credibility and oversight, we can empower them to specify for themselves what constitutes safe usage for teams or projects within their program."
Separately, Reuters reported on Friday that Anthropic has established its own laboratory to conduct physical biology work, citing people familiar with the matter.

"We believe that to do biology, the final ‌test is still and will be for a while in real lab work," said Eric Kaudere-Abrams, Anthropic's head of life sciences, in an interview with Reuters. "We absolutely are doing that today, and I would describe our approach as being typical of what you would see in most biotech companies, where there's some amount of that that we're doing in our own facilities and some amount of that ​that we're working with external partners on."
